35:1.ar: ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ فَاطِرِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ جَاعِلِ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ رُسُلًا أُوْلِيٓ أَجۡنِحَةࣲ مَّثۡنَىٰ وَثُلَٰثَ وَرُبَٰعَۚ يَزِيدُ فِي ٱلۡخَلۡقِ مَا يَشَآءُۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرࣱ‏
35:1.en: Praise be to Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will. Lo! Allah is Able to do all things

35:2.ar: مَّا يَفۡتَحِ ٱللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِن رَّحۡمَةࣲ فَلَا مُمۡسِكَ لَهَاۖ وَمَا يُمۡسِكۡ فَلَا مُرۡسِلَ لَهُۥ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦۚ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
35:2.en: That which Allah openeth unto mankind of mercy none can withhold it; and that which He withholdeth none can release thereafter. He is the Mighty, the Wise

39:6.ar: خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفۡسࣲ وَٰحِدَةࣲ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنۡهَا زَوۡجَهَا وَأَنزَلَ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ ثَمَٰنِيَةَ أَزۡوَٰجࣲۚ يَخۡلُقُكُمۡ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَٰتِكُمۡ خَلۡقࣰ ا مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ خَلۡقࣲ فِي ظُلُمَٰتࣲ ثَلَٰثࣲۚ ذَٰلِكُمُ ٱللَّهُ رَبُّكُمۡ لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُۖ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَۖ فَأَنَّىٰ تُصۡرَفُونَ
39:6.en: He created you from one being, then from that (being) He made its mate; and He hath provided for you of cattle eight kinds. He created you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in a threefold gloom. Such is Allah, your Lord. His is the Sovereignty. There is no Allah save Him. How then are ye turned away

38:26.ar: يَٰدَاوُۥدُ إِنَّا جَعَلۡنَٰكَ خَلِيفَةࣰ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ فَٱحۡكُم بَيۡنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَلَا تَتَّبِعِ ٱلۡهَوَىٰ فَيُضِلَّكَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَضِلُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ لَهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدُۢ بِمَا نَسُواْ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡحِسَابِ
38:26.en: (And it was said unto him): O David! Lo! We have set thee as a viceroy in the earth; therefor judge aright between mankind, and follow not desire that it beguile thee from the way of Allah. Lo! those who wander from the way of Allah have an awful doom, forasmuch as they forgot the Day of Reckoning

35:10.ar: مَن كَانَ يُرِيدُ ٱلۡعِزَّةَ فَلِلَّهِ ٱلۡعِزَّةُ جَمِيعًاۚ إِلَيۡهِ يَصۡعَدُ ٱلۡكَلِمُ ٱلطَّيِّبُ وَٱلۡعَمَلُ ٱلصَّٰلِحُ يَرۡفَعُهُۥۚ وَٱلَّذِينَ يَمۡكُرُونَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ لَهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدࣱۖ وَمَكۡرُ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُوَ يَبُورُ
35:10.en: Whoso desireth power (should know that) all power belongeth to Allah. Unto Him good words ascend, and the pious deed doth He exalt; but those who plot iniquities, theirs will be an awful doom; and the plotting of such (folk) will come to naught

7vGvepMWAlc.speaker_note: teaches the weekly Sunday English tafseer at the London Muslim Mosque, refers to the earlier surahs of the series and to his own father
7vGvepMWAlc.title: Tafseer of Surah Fatir, Session 1 (35:1-2)
7vGvepMWAlc.one_line: Opening of Surah Fatir: why the Quran is not spoon-fed, Allah's credentials for our submission, mercy no one can withhold, and knowing your role.
7vGvepMWAlc.summary: He opens by arguing that over-structured teaching bores the brain, while the Quran hands you puzzle pieces to connect, which is why it keeps yielding new findings. Even its order defies expectation: in this cluster of surahs on submission, Fatir, which explains why one should give up free will to Allah at all, comes third rather than first. He reads the first verse as Allah's resume. Fatir means the one who made the first break from nothing into being, a narrower word than general creation, so submitting to anyone else makes no sense. Angels are messengers who act without personal choice; the mention of their wings takes the Prophet back to seeing Jibril in his true form at the start of revelation, and reminds us how small and short-lived we are. The second verse teaches that no one can hold back mercy Allah sends or send what He withholds, which he links to the Ibn Abbas hadith and to accepting life's lows without resentment. A long tangent follows: know your role. Do not preach to a friend or parent who needs comfort, as Abu Hanifah let his mother ask another teacher and the Prophet lived as an ordinary husband with Aisha; being khalifah means playing many roles well, as Dawud did. He closes on al-Aziz al-Hakim.

outline.heading: The brain needs a puzzle, not spoon-feeding
outline.gist: Over-structured learning bores the brain and nothing sticks; people retain what they had to figure out, and the Quran is built to make you connect the dots.

outline.heading: The Quran's order defies expectation
outline.gist: The Quran does not start with faith, and this cluster of surahs on submission opens with the hardest stories instead of the reasons to submit, keeping the reader challenged.

outline.heading: Still finding new things after 1,400 years
outline.gist: Because the Quran is not a constitution of numbered articles, readers can still notice things no earlier tafsir recorded.

outline.heading: Why give up free will to Allah alone
outline.gist: Free will is the most precious thing you own and you surrender it to no human; Fatir is the surah that argues why Allah deserves it, how to do it and what follows.

outline.heading: Recitation of the opening verses
outline.gist: He recites the first two verses.

outline.heading: Allah presents His credentials
outline.gist: The surah opens by laying out who Allah is, as if handing over a resume to anyone still unsure whether He is worth submitting to.

outline.heading: The five surahs that open with praise
outline.gist: Fatir is one of the few surahs beginning with alhamdulillah, alongside al-Fatihah, al-An'am, al-Kahf and Saba, and there is a thread between them.

outline.heading: Fatir: the one who made the first break
outline.gist: The root means breaking or denting an untouched state, as in breaking a fast or the Bedouin who dug the first spade of a well; it is narrower than khalq, bara' or sawwara.

outline.heading: First reason to submit: He began everything
outline.gist: All that exists results from the moment Allah turned nothing into something, so there is no one else to submit to.

outline.heading: Angels as messengers without personal choice
outline.gist: Angels convey Allah's messages, verbal or physical, exactly as commanded; humans obey with a personal touch, so the two cannot be compared.

outline.heading: Wings and Jibril in his true form
outline.gist: The only Quranic mention of angels' wings recalls the Prophet seeing Jibril filling the horizon with six hundred wings at the start of revelation, a forceful yet tender beginning.

outline.heading: How small and simple we are
outline.gist: Allah increases His creation as He wills; next to the universe humans are physically tiny and fragile.

outline.heading: Sixty spins around the sun
outline.gist: Despite our smallness Allah gave us a mission; a lifetime is a few dozen trips around the sun to show whether we deserve an evolutionary step beyond imagination.

outline.heading: Mercy no one can withhold
outline.gist: Whatever mercy Allah opens to people, in any form, no one can hold back, and what He holds back no one can send.

outline.heading: The Ibn Abbas hadith: the pens are lifted
outline.gist: The Prophet taught the young Ibn Abbas that the whole world cannot benefit or harm you except with what Allah already wrote, the same idea as the verse.

outline.heading: Facing life's lows without resentment
outline.gist: At your lowest point this belief must kick in: accept it as your test and move forward instead of living in bitterness toward people and events.

outline.heading: Do not preach when you are meant to console
outline.gist: We learn the Quran to tell others what to do; a friend or son should comfort someone in pain, not lecture them, and leave preaching to those people listen to.

outline.heading: The tea shop owner who knows everything but tea
outline.gist: An anecdote about a tea seller who can fix parliament and cricket but cannot make good tea: identify your job and do it.

outline.heading: Abu Hanifah and his mother
outline.gist: The imam of his age was not his mother's teacher; she trusted a local knitter, and Abu Hanifah went to ask that man so his mother would accept the answer.

outline.heading: The Prophet as an ordinary husband
outline.gist: With Aisha the Prophet was a husband, not a preacher: he picked up the broken dish when she knocked it over out of jealousy and knew her moods by how she swore.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr and Umar could not accept it
outline.gist: Abu Bakr would scold Aisha and the Prophet stood between them, showing he played his roles of husband, father and friend differently.

outline.heading: Khalifah means playing many roles well
outline.gist: Each of you is a shepherd: stewardship carries versatility of roles, and the role most often failed is the friend who simply listens.

outline.heading: Dawud, the model khalifah
outline.gist: Dawud was king, judge, prophet, father, artisan, warrior and inventor, which is why he alone is called khalifah in the Quran.

outline.heading: Al-Aziz: the unfathomable
outline.gist: Al-Aziz means Allah can never be fully grasped, even in paradise; if you could figure God out He would not be God. The theme of izzah returns in verse 10.

outline.heading: Al-Hakim: no command without wisdom
outline.gist: Paired with al-Aziz, al-Hakim assures you that being beyond reach does not mean arbitrary; every command carries wisdom you may see later.

outline.heading: Recap: the case for submission
outline.gist: He sums up the two verses as the opening argument for submission and points to the commands that begin in the next verse addressed to all people.

48:27.en: Allah hath fulfilled the vision for His messenger in very truth. Ye shall indeed enter the Inviolable Place of Worship, if Allah will, secure, (having your hair) shaven and cut, not fearing. But He knoweth that which ye know not, and hath given you a near victory beforehand

iQqfn3ofNeU.title: Seerah Halaqah: Expeditions of Year Six and the Road to Hudaybiyyah (Part 2)
iQqfn3ofNeU.one_line: Year six expeditions: the whale at Sif al-Bahr, Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf's mission and the Prophet's rules of war, raids on Medina, and choosing peace.
iQqfn3ofNeU.summary: The sheikh explains that after the Trench the Prophet pressured Quraysh's caravans for one goal: freedom to speak to the tribes without Quraysh frightening them away. He tells of the expedition to the coast where starving companions found a beached whale, ate from it for days and brought meat back to the Prophet, and uses it to explain that dead sea creatures are lawful. He then recounts the mission of Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf to Dumat al-Jandal, where the Prophet tied his turban for him and gave rules of war: fight only for Allah, do not steal, do not betray even an enemy, do not kill non-combatants. He adds the Prophet's warning about five sins and their consequences: cheating in trade brings poverty, betraying covenants invites enemies, withholding zakat stops blessing, spreading zina brings disease, and abandoning the Quran brings division. The sheikh stresses these are natural consequences, not mythical punishments. From year six, Muslims were attacked repeatedly, as in Uyaynah's raid on the Prophet's camels and the Uraynah men who killed his shepherds. Even so, once the Prophet held the initiative he chose peace, and his dream of entering Mecca became a plan to use the sacred truce of pilgrimage.

outline.heading: Pressuring Quraysh's caravans for freedom to speak
outline.gist: Expeditions near the coast pressured Quraysh, whose threats kept tribes from listening to the Prophet.

outline.heading: All he asked for was the right to speak
outline.gist: The Prophet forced no one; he wanted only that people be allowed to hear him.

outline.heading: The whale on the shore at Sif al-Bahr
outline.gist: Starving companions find a huge beached whale, eat from it until they regain weight, and bring some back to the Prophet.

outline.heading: Two dead things and two bloods are lawful
outline.gist: Dead fish and locusts, liver and spleen are permitted; sea creatures need no slaughter if the meat is not spoiled.

outline.heading: Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf sent to Dumat al-Jandal
outline.gist: A northern group was funding fighters against Medina; he is sent to end it or invite them to Islam.

outline.heading: The Prophet ties his turban
outline.gist: Before leaving, the Prophet wraps his turban with a tail between his shoulders, a relic he kept for years.

outline.heading: Rules of war: no theft, betrayal or killing non-combatants
outline.gist: Fight in Allah's name and only those who fight; do not steal, break agreements, or harm children and the elderly.

outline.heading: Five sins and their consequences: cheating in trade
outline.gist: When people cheat in measures, years of poverty follow as a natural result of financial corruption.

outline.heading: Betraying covenants invites enemies
outline.gist: A society without trust is easily overrun by its enemies.

outline.heading: Withholding zakat stops the rain of blessing
outline.gist: When the poor go hungry there is no blessing in a community.

outline.heading: When indecency spreads, disease follows
outline.gist: Without lowering the gaze and making marriage easy, zina spreads and brings disease and weakness.

outline.heading: Abandoning the Quran brings division
outline.gist: When the Quran stops guiding daily life, Muslims split into quarrelling groups; the warnings came true.

outline.heading: Constant raids on Muslims from year six
outline.gist: Muslims on caravans and in pastures were killed repeatedly, which explains later rulings on securing the area.

outline.heading: Uyaynah's raid on the Prophet's camels
outline.gist: Raiders kill a companion's son, seize camels and his wife; the companions pursue and recover them.

outline.heading: The woman's vow to slaughter the camel that saved her
outline.gist: The Prophet objects: there is no vow in disobedience or in what you do not own, and the camel saved her life.

outline.heading: The Uraynah men kill the Prophet's shepherds
outline.gist: Men who feigned interest in Islam mutilated and killed the shepherds; the Prophet wept over them.

outline.heading: With the initiative in hand, he chooses peace
outline.gist: Quraysh chose war whenever they could; the Prophet, now stronger, chose peace.

outline.heading: A new, impulsive but open generation in Quraysh
outline.gist: Younger leaders lacked their fathers' wisdom but were more open, giving the Prophet hope.

outline.heading: The dream of entering Mecca
outline.gist: He dreams of entering the Sacred Mosque with heads shaved or trimmed and sees how to force peace.

outline.heading: The sacred truce of pilgrimage
outline.gist: In Arabia no one could be stopped from umrah or hajj, and even enemies laid down arms.

4:43.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَقۡرَبُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأَنتُمۡ سُكَٰرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ تَعۡلَمُواْ مَا تَقُولُونَ وَلَا جُنُبًا إِلَّا عَابِرِي سَبِيلٍ حَتَّىٰ تَغۡتَسِلُواْۚ وَإِن كُنتُم مَّرۡضَىٰٓ أَوۡ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ أَوۡ جَآءَ أَحَدࣱ مِّنكُم مِّنَ ٱلۡغَآئِطِ أَوۡ لَٰمَسۡتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَلَمۡ تَجِدُواْ مَآءࣰ فَتَيَمَّمُواْ صَعِيدࣰ ا طَيِّبࣰ ا فَٱمۡسَحُواْ بِوُجُوهِكُمۡ وَأَيۡدِيكُمۡۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَفُوًّا غَفُورًا
4:43.en: O ye who believe! Draw not near unto prayer when ye are drunken, till ye know that which ye utter, nor when ye are polluted, save when journeying upon the road, till ye have bathed. And if ye be ill, or on a journey, or one of you cometh from the closet, or ye have touched women, and ye find not water, then go to high clean soil and rub your faces and your hands (therewith). Lo! Allah is Benign, Forgiving

3KsBJGGZKiA.title: Seerah Halaqah: Digging the Trench (Part 3)
3KsBJGGZKiA.one_line: The hardships of digging the trench, the Prophet's labour and leadership, the prohibition of intoxicants just before it, and poetry to lift morale.
3KsBJGGZKiA.summary: The sheikh opens with his own attempt to dig one man's share of the trench with ten volunteers, which took them a week, to show how hard the task was. He lists the three problems the companions faced: intense fear, described in Surat al-Ahzab as a psychological earthquake; a strict deadline; and hunger in a lean season. He recounts Jabir's report of the Prophet carrying dirt with his stomach tied tight from hunger, choosing the hardest job, visiting all sixty groups daily to raise morale, and inspecting the work from Mount Sal'. He then turns to the prohibition of khamr revealed shortly before the Trench, explaining that anything that intoxicates recreationally is forbidden, while medical use prescribed by a physician, such as anaesthesia, is different. He extends this to smoking, which is forbidden because it causes direct harm, and urges young people to avoid vaping and protect their lungs. The companions' immediate obedience, pouring their wine into the streets, shows a community that had learned from earlier disobedience. Finally he argues that a tired, hungry, frightened community needs art to lift its spirits: the Prophet called on poets like Ibn Rawahah and joined their chanting by repeating the last word of each line.

outline.gist: Ten volunteers took a week to dig the share of a single companion, showing how hard the task was.

outline.gist: The believers were shaken as if by an earthquake when they heard ten thousand were coming.

outline.heading: Second problem: finishing on time
outline.gist: A half-finished trench, or exhausted defenders, would make the effort worthless.

outline.heading: Third problem: hunger
outline.gist: It was a lean season after much wealth had left Medina, while men worked long days.

outline.heading: Jabir sees the Prophet carrying dirt
outline.gist: The Prophet carried earth all day, his stomach bound tightly from hunger.

outline.heading: The Prophet takes the hardest job and visits every group
outline.gist: He refused easier work and spent time with each of the sixty groups to keep morale up.

outline.heading: Quality inspections from Mount Sal'
outline.gist: He checked the whole line for width and depth; the companions never saw him so tired.

outline.heading: Prohibition of intoxicants just before the Trench
outline.gist: After the disobedience at Uhud, the ban on khamr tested whether the community would obey immediately.

outline.heading: Every recreational intoxicant is forbidden
outline.gist: Khamr is whatever veils the mind; alcohol, drugs and marijuana used for fun are all forbidden.

outline.heading: Medical intoxicants decided by physicians
outline.gist: Anaesthesia and prescribed drugs, including medical marijuana, are different when a doctor diagnoses and doses them.

outline.heading: Smoking forbidden because of direct harm
outline.gist: Cigarettes are not intoxicants but cause cancers; whatever directly harms you is forbidden.

outline.heading: Do not approach prayer intoxicated
outline.gist: We do not give up sobriety unless medically necessary; Allah does not want to be addressed with half a mind.

outline.heading: Vaping and protecting your body
outline.gist: He doubts claims vaping is harmless, cites lung injuries in young people, and urges them to protect lungs, liver and brain.

outline.heading: The companions pour out their wine
outline.gist: On hearing the ban they emptied their homes of wine and never drank again, having learned from past disobedience.

outline.heading: Morale and the community's need for art
outline.gist: Tired, hungry and scared people need art to lift them; a community without art cannot endure hard times.

outline.heading: Ibn Rawahah's poetry at the trench
outline.gist: The Prophet calls on poets, and the verses asking Allah for guidance, tranquillity and steadfastness are chanted.

outline.heading: The Prophet repeats the last word of each line
outline.gist: Unable to keep a tune, he joined by stretching the final word, and the whole army followed.

gb6E7QOP8w4.title: Seerah Halaqah: The Prophet's Win-Win Plan for Umrah (Part 3)
gb6E7QOP8w4.one_line: How the Prophet designed the umrah journey toward Hudaybiyyah so every outcome favoured peace, and his words about Quraysh being consumed by war.
gb6E7QOP8w4.summary: The sheikh explains the logic of the Prophet's plan to go for umrah. Whatever Quraysh did, he would win: if they let the Muslims in, all Arabia would see that the hostility was over and listen freely; if they turned pilgrims away, the tribes would sympathise with him; and if they negotiated a treaty, the fighting would stop and other tribes could listen. The only way to lose was a battle, so he took steps to avoid one. He travelled in a sacred month when even idolaters held fighting forbidden, brought sacrificial animals so everyone could see he came for worship, carried only travellers' swords without heavy armour, and invited non-Muslims of Medina along to show this was not a Muslim war party. Quraysh still sent Khalid ibn al-Walid with cavalry to block him, so the Prophet changed route. The sheikh highlights the Prophet's lament that war had consumed Quraysh, and his argument that letting him speak to people could only benefit them: if others defeated him, Quraysh got what they wanted; if he prevailed, they could join with honour. He resolves to keep calling until Allah grants victory, which the sheikh presents as proof of his peaceful intent.

outline.heading: Three outcomes, all wins
outline.gist: Being let in, turned back, or offered a treaty would each open Arabia to his message.

outline.heading: Avoid war: travel in the sacred months
outline.gist: A battle was the only way to lose, so he chose a month in which even idolaters forbade fighting.

outline.heading: Sacrificial animals and light arms
outline.gist: Herds of sacrificial animals and the absence of armour showed everyone he came to worship.

outline.heading: Inviting non-Muslims of Medina along
outline.gist: He took Medina's idolaters too, so it was clearly not a Muslim war party.

outline.heading: Ihram, and Quraysh sends Khalid's cavalry
outline.gist: The pilgrims set out ready for ihram; Quraysh immediately send Khalid ibn al-Walid to block them outside Mecca.

outline.heading: Changing route and the Prophet's lament
outline.gist: Learning of Quraysh's resolve, he takes another route and says war has consumed Quraysh.

outline.heading: Let me speak to people: no way for Quraysh to lose
outline.gist: If others defeat him, Quraysh gain; if he prevails, they can join with honour; he will keep calling until victory.

outline.heading: Outro

35:10.ar: مَن كَانَ يُرِيدُ ٱلۡعِزَّةَ فَلِلَّهِ ٱلۡعِزَّةُ جَمِيعًاۚ إِلَيۡهِ يَصۡعَدُ ٱلۡكَلِمُ ٱلطَّيِّبُ وَٱلۡعَمَلُ ٱلصَّٰلِحُ يَرۡفَعُهُۥۚ وَٱلَّذِينَ يَمۡكُرُونَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ لَهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدࣱۖ وَمَكۡرُ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُوَ يَبُورُ
35:10.en: Whoso desireth power (should know that) all power belongeth to Allah. Unto Him good words ascend, and the pious deed doth He exalt; but those who plot iniquities, theirs will be an awful doom; and the plotting of such (folk) will come to naught

35:11.ar: وَٱللَّهُ خَلَقَكُم مِّن تُرَابࣲ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطۡفَةࣲ ثُمَّ جَعَلَكُمۡ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ اۚ وَمَا تَحۡمِلُ مِنۡ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ إِلَّا بِعِلۡمِهِۦۚ وَمَا يُعَمَّرُ مِن مُّعَمَّرࣲ وَلَا يُنقَصُ مِنۡ عُمُرِهِۦٓ إِلَّا فِي كِتَٰبٍۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرࣱ‏
35:11.en: Allah created you from dust, then from a little fluid, then He made you pairs (the male and female). No female beareth or bringeth forth save with His knowledge. And no-one groweth old who groweth old, nor is aught lessened of his life, but it is recorded in a Book, Lo! that is easy for Allah

35:3.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡۚ هَلۡ مِنۡ خَٰلِقٍ غَيۡرُ ٱللَّهِ يَرۡزُقُكُم مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَۖ فَأَنَّىٰ تُؤۡفَكُونَ
35:3.en: O mankind! Remember Allah's grace toward you! Is there any creator other than Allah who provideth for you from the sky and the earth? There is no Allah save Him. Whither then are ye turned

35:4.ar: وَإِن يُكَذِّبُوكَ فَقَدۡ كُذِّبَتۡ رُسُلࣱ مِّن قَبۡلِكَۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرۡجَعُ ٱلۡأُمُورُ
35:4.en: And if they deny thee, (O Muhammad), messengers (of Allah) were denied before thee. Unto Allah all things are brought back

35:5.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّۖ فَلَا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكُم بِٱللَّهِ ٱلۡغَرُورُ
35:5.en: O mankind! Lo! the promise of Allah is true. So let not the life of the world beguile you, and let not the (avowed) beguiler beguile you with regard to Allah

35:6.ar: إِنَّ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنَ لَكُمۡ عَدُوࣱّ فَٱتَّخِذُوهُ عَدُوًّاۚ إِنَّمَا يَدۡعُواْ حِزۡبَهُۥ لِيَكُونُواْ مِنۡ أَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلسَّعِيرِ
35:6.en: Lo! the devil is an enemy for you, so treat him as an enemy. He only summoneth his faction to be owners of the flaming Fire

35:7.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لَهُمۡ عَذَابࣱ شَدِيدࣱۖ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ لَهُم مَّغۡفِرَةࣱ وَأَجۡرࣱ كَبِيرٌ
35:7.en: Those who disbelieve, theirs will be an awful doom; and those who believe and do good works, theirs will be forgiveness and a great reward

35:8.ar: أَفَمَن زُيِّنَ لَهُۥ سُوٓءُ عَمَلِهِۦ فَرَءَاهُ حَسَنࣰ اۖ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُضِلُّ مَن يَشَآءُ وَيَهۡدِي مَن يَشَآءُۖ فَلَا تَذۡهَبۡ نَفۡسُكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ حَسَرَٰتٍۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمُۢ بِمَا يَصۡنَعُونَ
35:8.en: Is he, the evil of whose deeds is made fairseeming unto him so that he deemeth it good, (other than Satan's dupe)? Allah verily sendeth whom He will astray, and guideth whom He will; so let not thy soul expire in sighings for them. Lo! Allah is Aware of what they do

35:9.ar: وَٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِيٓ أَرۡسَلَ ٱلرِّيَٰحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابࣰ ا فَسُقۡنَٰهُ إِلَىٰ بَلَدࣲ مَّيِّتࣲ فَأَحۡيَيۡنَا بِهِ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ بَعۡدَ مَوۡتِهَاۚ كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ
35:9.en: And Allah it is Who sendeth the winds and they raise a cloud; then We lead it unto a dead land and revive therewith the earth after its death. Such is the Resurrection

4:139.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَّخِذُونَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ أَوۡلِيَآءَ مِن دُونِ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَۚ أَيَبۡتَغُونَ عِندَهُمُ ٱلۡعِزَّةَ فَإِنَّ ٱلۡعِزَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا
4:139.en: Those who chose disbelievers for their friends instead of believers! Do they look for power at their hands? Lo! all power appertaineth to Allah

53:16.en: When that which shroudeth did enshroud the lote-tree

13:29.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ طُوبَىٰ لَهُمۡ وَحُسۡنُ مَـَٔابࣲ‏
13:29.en: Those who believe and do right: Joy is for them, and bliss (their) journey's end

16:97.ar: مَنۡ عَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ ا مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوۡ أُنثَىٰ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنࣱ فَلَنُحۡيِيَنَّهُۥ حَيَوٰةࣰ طَيِّبَةࣰۖ وَلَنَجۡزِيَنَّهُمۡ أَجۡرَهُم بِأَحۡسَنِ مَا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ
16:97.en: Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life, and We shall pay them a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do

0IqupWggDVM.speaker: adnan
0IqupWggDVM.speaker_note: continues his Sunday English tafseer of Fatir and answers a question an attendee had asked him in an earlier session
0IqupWggDVM.title: Tafseer of Surah Fatir, Session 4 (35:10-11)
0IqupWggDVM.one_line: Whoever wants izzah, all of it belongs to Allah: good words and deeds raise you, evil plots come to nothing, and Allah's foreknowledge explained.
0IqupWggDVM.summary: He recaps the two mindsets needed for submission, gratitude and self-insight, then takes up a question an attendee raised: what about the human urge for dignity and greatness, which seems to clash with surrendering to Allah? Verse 10 answers it. After grouping Allah's names into families, he explains al-Aziz as the unreachable and unfathomable, which is why it accompanies punishment we cannot fully understand. Wanting izzah is natural and the verse validates it, but all of it belongs to Allah, so seeking it from money, land, family or regimes yields a fake that war or calamity exposes. True izzah is an inner value, like the hero who stays upright under torture. Good words rise to Allah, and in his preferred reading good deeds raise the person's own standing; kind speech looks weak but is the real source of dignity, while words without deeds are hypocrisy. Those who plot to get ahead will see their plotting crumble. Verse 11 traces human creation and lifespans to a record, which he explains as Allah's prior knowledge rather than compulsion: the record is unseen, knowledge does not cause action, a God who could be surprised would not deserve worship, and Allah knows outcomes even of free choices.

outline.heading: Recap: gratitude and self-insight
outline.gist: Fatir has no stories because it presents a way of seeing; so far it has given Allah's credentials and the two mindsets of submission, explained through insight in verse 8 and resurrection in verse 9.

outline.heading: The question: what about our urge for dignity?
outline.gist: An attendee asked about self-pride: we all want to be the best and held in high esteem, which seems to pull against laying ourselves down before Allah's will.

outline.heading: The Quran answers questions if you reflect
outline.gist: If you think about what you are told and stay patient, the Quran raises and answers your questions in turn and stops feeling disconnected.

outline.heading: Recitation
outline.gist: He recites verses 10 and 11 and drills the hard sequence of three doubled mims in verse 11.

outline.heading: Grouping the names of Allah
outline.gist: He groups names into families, such as those under al-Alim, while names like al-Hakim stand alone; without al-Hakim we could not be sure every command benefits us.

outline.heading: Al-Aziz: what is beyond reach
outline.gist: Scholars give a dozen definitions, but every derivative of the root shares one meaning: something hard to reach.

outline.heading: Reading people, and being read
outline.gist: Social skill lets you read people and psychologists can break you down to your basics, a humbling experience everyone should have once.

outline.heading: Can we figure God out?
outline.gist: Atheists and makers of personal gods think they have figured God out; al-Aziz says His essence is beyond reach even mentally.

outline.heading: Why al-Aziz accompanies punishment
outline.gist: Rather than a name of strength, he reads al-Aziz with punishment as a sign that we will never fully understand why punishment must exist.

outline.heading: The Prophet at the Lote Tree
outline.gist: Even the most articulate of people could not describe what covered the Lote Tree; you can understand Allah's law, never His essence.

outline.heading: What we want when we want izzah
outline.gist: Izzah at its simplest means no one can grab you by the collar; we also want esteem and respect, which seems the opposite of submission.

outline.heading: All izzah has one source
outline.gist: Wanting izzah is natural, but it is like a product only one maker produces: get it elsewhere and you have a fake.

outline.heading: Fake izzah exposed by war
outline.gist: A man whose standing rested on land, sons or a regime can be left with nothing in a moment; if his izzah came from Allah he still has it.

outline.heading: Izzah as an inner value
outline.gist: Self-worth that comes from walking Allah's path stands even under torture, which is why a film hero who breaks under torture makes no sense.

outline.heading: The verse validates the pursuit of izzah
outline.gist: Allah does not say stop wanting it; He says it is all His, so pursue it through Him and He grants it by your attachment to His teaching.

outline.heading: Good words ascend to Him
outline.gist: Every kind and good word or saying rises to Allah.

outline.heading: Who raises what: the traditional readings
outline.gist: Either Allah raises good deeds, or good deeds raise the good words even higher; both readings are found in the books of tafsir.

outline.heading: His reading: deeds raise your status
outline.gist: He prefers that righteous deeds raise the person himself; that, not money or social status, is what lifts you up.

outline.heading: Tayyib: wholesome and good
outline.gist: Tayyib is the opposite of rotting, the root behind Taybah as a name of Madinah and the good life of the content believer who knows why things happen.

outline.heading: Kind words look weak but bring izzah
outline.gist: Speaking kindly usually feels like being walked over and kings never need to; yet it is the true source of izzah, and words without deeds would be hypocrisy.

outline.heading: Gentleness beautifies everything
outline.gist: The hadith that gentleness adorns anything it enters and its removal disfigures it.

outline.heading: Those who plot to get ahead
outline.gist: Seekers of worldly izzah plot to bring rivals down through gossip and backstabbing; their plotting will turn to nothing like barren land, so be patient.

outline.heading: Seek izzah in kindness and good deeds
outline.gist: The answer to the question is to seek dignity in Allah's pleasure and good deeds; it is odd to see Muslim professionals climbing through rudeness.

outline.heading: From dust to a recorded lifespan
outline.gist: Created from dust, then a drop, then made pairs; every pregnancy and birth is known, and no life is lengthened or shortened except in a record.

outline.heading: Kitab means prior knowledge, not compulsion
outline.gist: Being in a record means it was known beforehand, not that you contributed nothing; he is surprised how many older Muslims still struggle with this.

outline.heading: Does the writing bother you?
outline.gist: If it were not written you would be at ease, yet no one has seen the Preserved Tablet; the records angels see do change, as kinship ties lengthen life.

outline.heading: A God who could be surprised is not worth worship
outline.gist: If Allah did not know what comes next He could be beaten; knowing the future would also remove anxiety, which shows the strength in knowledge.

outline.heading: Knowledge does not cause action
outline.gist: Whether or not you know that chickens lay eggs, they still lay them; Allah's knowledge does not make your choice for you.

outline.heading: He knows how it ends, so follow Him
outline.gist: Because everything from the first cell to every lifespan is recorded, Allah can promise that kindness raises you and plots fail; what matters is izzah on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Our knowledge needs programming, His does not
outline.gist: We predict only what we program or estimate statistically, as insurers do; Allah knows which wall you will hit even though you choose freely, which is why He is God.

outline.heading: Outro

mk0rm4qVC4c.title: Seerah Halaqah, October 20, 2018 (Part 1): Lessons from Dhat al-Riqa'
mk0rm4qVC4c.one_line: Reviewing Dhat al-Riqa': the Prophet's restraint, prayer with no excuse, choosing peace over bloodshed, doing things well, and the guard who kept reciting.
mk0rm4qVC4c.summary: He places the class in the timeline, the fifth year after the Hijrah, and explains why the Medinan years need slower treatment. Tribes were breaking treaties and killing innocent Muslims, yet the Prophet refused to be dragged into endless wars; he defused situations, did not seek revenge, and showed strength only where needed to protect morale and reputation. He notes that the Prophet never separated inner and outer: a clean heart and clean clothes go together. He then reviews Dhat al-Riqa'. The fear prayer shows prayer is not dropped even in war; only true emergencies, like a surgeon mid-operation or a pilot in a storm, justify delaying it, so carry what you need to pray anywhere. The man who held the Prophet's sword to his neck was released without punishment, and the Prophet always chose the option without bloodshed, a mindset he links to how Islam spread. Posting guards properly the next night leads to a rule he repeats often: whatever you do, do it well, instead of pretending to study or work. He ends with the guard who was struck by three arrows while praying and kept going because he would not cut short the surah he was enjoying, urging listeners to build that closeness to the Quran gradually.

outline.heading: Opening
Where we are in the timeline
outline.gist: Thirteen years in Mecca and ten in Medina; they are in the fifth Medinan year, which needs slower, more detailed treatment.

outline.heading: Broken treaties and murdered Muslims

outline.heading: Not getting dragged into every war

outline.heading: Inner and outer never separated
outline.gist: The Prophet joined a clean heart with clean clothes; only extreme poverty might force a choice between them.

outline.heading: Recap: the march of the rags

outline.heading: The fear prayer means no excuse
outline.gist: Teaching prayer during war indirectly tells us we may not skip prayer for work or school.

outline.heading: The few real exceptions
outline.gist: Only emergencies like a surgeon mid-operation or a pilot in a storm justify postponing a prayer; school, work and shopping do not.

outline.heading: Be prepared to pray anywhere
outline.gist: Carry what you need, since masjids are not everywhere; the enemy fled and the army stayed a night to show strength.

outline.heading: Recap: the man with the sword went unpunished
outline.gist: He came to kill, not to argue, yet the Prophet asked only that he never fight the Muslims and let him go.

outline.heading: Always choose the option without bloodshed
outline.gist: Given two options, the Prophet chose peace; the early Muslims did not enter lands with a mindset of killing.

outline.heading: Posting the guard properly
outline.gist: After the first lapse, the Prophet organised the watch more carefully the next night.

outline.heading: Whatever you do, do it well
outline.gist: Do not act as if you are studying while your mind is elsewhere; doing things with excellence is the essence of ihsan.

outline.heading: Two companions share the night watch
outline.gist: They split the night; one slept while the other stood guard and prayed facing the side the enemy might come from.

outline.heading: Three arrows during the prayer
outline.gist: A hidden enemy shot him three times; he pulled the arrows out and kept praying until the wounds forced him to wake his companion.

outline.heading: Rather die than cut the surah short
outline.gist: He explained he was enjoying his recitation so much that he would sooner lose his life than stop.

outline.heading: Build that closeness slowly
outline.gist: No one expects that level of joy at once; start building your relationship with the Book of Allah gradually now.

18:9.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتَ أَنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡكَهۡفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُواْ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا عَجَبًا
18:9.en: Or deemest thou that the People of the Cave and the Inscription are a wonder among Our portents

18:10.ar: إِذۡ أَوَى ٱلۡفِتۡيَةُ إِلَى ٱلۡكَهۡفِ فَقَالُواْ رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحۡمَةࣰ وَهَيِّئۡ لَنَا مِنۡ أَمۡرِنَا رَشَدࣰ ا
18:10.en: When the young men fled for refuge to the Cave and said: Our Lord! Give us mercy from Thy presence, and shape for us right conduct in our plight

18:11.ar: فَضَرَبۡنَا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاذَانِهِمۡ فِي ٱلۡكَهۡفِ سِنِينَ عَدَدࣰ ا
18:11.en: Then We sealed up their hearing in the Cave for a number of years

18:12.ar: ثُمَّ بَعَثۡنَٰهُمۡ لِنَعۡلَمَ أَيُّ ٱلۡحِزۡبَيۡنِ أَحۡصَىٰ لِمَا لَبِثُوٓاْ أَمَدࣰ ا
18:12.en: And afterward We raised them up that We might know which of the two parties would best calculate the time that they had tarried

18:13.ar: نَّحۡنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيۡكَ نَبَأَهُم بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ إِنَّهُمۡ فِتۡيَةٌ ءَامَنُواْ بِرَبِّهِمۡ وَزِدۡنَٰهُمۡ هُدࣰ ى
18:13.en: We narrate unto thee their story with truth. Lo! they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance

18:14.ar: وَرَبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ إِذۡ قَامُواْ فَقَالُواْ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ لَن نَّدۡعُوَاْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَٰهࣰ اۖ لَّقَدۡ قُلۡنَآ إِذࣰ ا شَطَطًا
18:14.en: And We made firm their hearts when they stood forth and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We cry unto no Allah beside Him, for then should we utter an enormity

18:15.ar: هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ قَوۡمُنَا ٱتَّخَذُواْ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ ءَالِهَةࣰۖ لَّوۡلَا يَأۡتُونَ عَلَيۡهِم بِسُلۡطَٰنِۭ بَيِّنࣲۖ فَمَنۡ أَظۡلَمُ مِمَّنِ ٱفۡتَرَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ كَذِبࣰ ا
18:15.en: These, our people, have chosen (other) gods beside Him though they bring no clear warrant (vouchsafed) to them. And who doth greater wrong than he who inventeth a lie concerning Allah

18:16.ar: وَإِذِ ٱعۡتَزَلۡتُمُوهُمۡ وَمَا يَعۡبُدُونَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهَ فَأۡوُۥٓاْ إِلَى ٱلۡكَهۡفِ يَنشُرۡ لَكُمۡ رَبُّكُم مِّن رَّحۡمَتِهِۦ وَيُهَيِّئۡ لَكُم مِّنۡ أَمۡرِكُم مِّرۡفَقࣰ ا
18:16.en: And when ye withdraw from them and that which they worship except Allah, then seek refuge in the Cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a pillow in your plight

18:17.ar: ۞وَتَرَى ٱلشَّمۡسَ إِذَا طَلَعَت تَّزَٰوَرُ عَن كَهۡفِهِمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَت تَّقۡرِضُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ وَهُمۡ فِي فَجۡوَةࣲ مِّنۡهُۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۗ مَن يَهۡدِ ٱللَّهُ فَهُوَ ٱلۡمُهۡتَدِۖ وَمَن يُضۡلِلۡ فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ وَلِيࣰّ ا مُّرۡشِدࣰ ا
18:17.en: And thou mightest have seen the sun when it rose move away from their cave to the right, and when it set go past them on the left, and they were in the cleft thereof. That was (one) of the portents of Allah. He whom Allah guideth, he indeed is led aright, and he whom He sendeth astray, for him thou wilt not find a guiding friend

18:18.ar: وَتَحۡسَبُهُمۡ أَيۡقَاظࣰ ا وَهُمۡ رُقُودࣱۚ وَنُقَلِّبُهُمۡ ذَاتَ ٱلۡيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِۖ وَكَلۡبُهُم بَٰسِطࣱ ذِرَاعَيۡهِ بِٱلۡوَصِيدِۚ لَوِ ٱطَّلَعۡتَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لَوَلَّيۡتَ مِنۡهُمۡ فِرَارࣰ ا وَلَمُلِئۡتَ مِنۡهُمۡ رُعۡبࣰ ا
18:18.en: And thou wouldst have deemed them waking though they were asleep, and We caused them to turn over to the right and the left, and their dog stretching out his paws on the threshold. If thou hadst observed them closely thou hadst assuredly turned away from them in flight, and hadst been filled with awe of them

NDrgPtcvGhk.title: Seerah Halaqah, October 20, 2018 (Part 2): Joy in the Quran and Jabir's Camel
NDrgPtcvGhk.one_line: A guard who would not stop reciting while struck by arrows, how to fall in love with the Quran, and the Prophet cheering Jabir on the road home.
NDrgPtcvGhk.summary: He continues with the return from Dhat al-Riqa'. A companion standing guard at night was struck by arrows while praying and kept reciting, because he was so absorbed in the story of the youths of the cave that the pain did not matter. Using the image of refusing to leave a warm bed when the alarm rings, he asks whether we have ever felt that kind of joy in the Quran. Loving the Quran takes time and effort; nobody can force love into a heart, but reading, understanding and living its stories opens the way, and whoever reaches it carries a lasting happiness and draws others to the book. He then tells the story of Jabir ibn Abdullah, whose father was killed at Uhud leaving him nine sisters to support, trailing at the back on a worn-out camel. The Prophet sought him out, revived the camel, bargained to buy it, and lifted his spirits. That the Prophet did not even know Jabir had married shows how simple marriage was then. He contrasts this with today, when young people wait a decade past puberty, and calls on families to make marriage easy, prepare young people for it, keep the mahr reasonable and look for character over wealth.

outline.heading: A guard who would not cut his recitation
outline.gist: Struck by arrows while praying at night, the companion felt such peace with Allah that he did not want to stop.

outline.heading: Like refusing to leave a warm bed
outline.gist: Everyone knows the joy of one more minute of sleep; he asks whether we have felt that in worship.

outline.heading: Living the story of the youths of the cave
outline.gist: He was so immersed in Surat al-Kahf that an arrow was just a wound to deal with after the story ended.

outline.heading: Loving the Quran takes work
outline.gist: It does not happen overnight, but once you love it you can renew your happiness simply by reciting; he fears for anyone not working toward it.

outline.heading: The visitor at the masjid open house
outline.gist: An elderly visitor was amazed that every book on the shelves was the same book; one book is all we need.

outline.heading: Words on a page until they reach the heart
outline.gist: The Quran changes people only when mixed with intellect, spirit and understanding, as it transformed the first generation.

outline.heading: Like a novel you cannot put down
outline.gist: The companion was living the story the way a reader gets lost near the end of a gripping novel.

outline.heading: Enjoying a good recitation
outline.gist: Being able to sit and enjoy someone's recitation is one of the best things you can do; reach that and much else stops worrying you.

outline.heading: Love cannot be forced
outline.gist: Teachers can teach words and expose you, but love is in the heart; you educate yourself and hope the feeling grows.

outline.heading: Learn to read it and bring others to it
outline.gist: Reading and understanding opens the way to love, and the one who loves the Quran draws others to it.

outline.heading: Researching Jabir's story in the library
outline.gist: He recalls spending weeks in a university library tracing every narration of this well-authenticated story.

outline.heading: The road home and the Prophet among the groups
outline.gist: Spirits were high on the return; the Prophet moved from group to group talking with people.

outline.heading: Who Jabir was
outline.gist: His father died at Uhud and wished to be returned to be martyred again, leaving Jabir alone with nine sisters.

outline.heading: Jabir at the back on a slow camel
outline.gist: While others laughed and talked, Jabir trailed behind until the Prophet came to ask what was wrong.

outline.heading: What a camel meant
outline.gist: A healthy camel was costly and did everything for you, like owning a car.

outline.heading: The Prophet revives the camel and buys it
outline.gist: Jabir was low and broke; the Prophet prodded the camel into speed and playfully bargained to buy it.

outline.heading: He always looked for the lonely one
outline.gist: Even on a march the Prophet searched for whoever was down or alone and found a way to make them smile.

outline.heading: Just be a good friend
outline.gist: The lesson is simple: say something kind, lift someone's mood, be a good neighbour.

outline.heading: The Prophet did not know Jabir had married
outline.gist: Marriage was so simple then, financially, socially and religiously, that it passed without notice in a small city.

outline.heading: A decade between puberty and marriage
outline.gist: Most young people today marry around 25, and the community prefers not to ask what happens in those years.

outline.heading: Respect for young people holding themselves back
outline.gist: He worries for the future and respects every unmarried young person keeping chaste under this pressure.

outline.heading: Families must find solutions now
outline.gist: Prepare youth psychologically and socially for marriage, help them financially, and keep the mahr feasible.

outline.heading: Look for decent, moral Muslims
outline.gist: Families should seek character, not wealth; Jabir's wedding was so quick it was not an event.

outline.heading: The fantasy of the perfect wedding
outline.gist: Raising daughters around one dream day, and young men around unrealistic expectations, is not healthy.

4:105.ar: إِنَّآ أَنزَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ لِتَحۡكُمَ بَيۡنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِمَآ أَرَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُۚ وَلَا تَكُن لِّلۡخَآئِنِينَ خَصِيمࣰ ا
4:105.en: Lo! We reveal unto thee the Scripture with the truth, that thou mayst judge between mankind by that which Allah showeth thee. And be not thou a pleader for the treacherous

4:106.ar: وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرِ ٱللَّهَۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ غَفُورࣰ ا رَّحِيمࣰ ا
4:106.en: And seek forgiveness of Allah. Lo! Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful

4:107.ar: وَلَا تُجَٰدِلۡ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخۡتَانُونَ أَنفُسَهُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ مَن كَانَ خَوَّانًا أَثِيمࣰ ا
4:107.en: And plead not on behalf of (people) who deceive themselves. Lo! Allah loveth not one who is treacherous and sinful

4:108.ar: يَسۡتَخۡفُونَ مِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَا يَسۡتَخۡفُونَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ وَهُوَ مَعَهُمۡ إِذۡ يُبَيِّتُونَ مَا لَا يَرۡضَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡلِۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِمَا يَعۡمَلُونَ مُحِيطًا
4:108.en: They seek to hide from men and seek not to hide from Allah. He is with them when by night they hold discourse displeasing unto Him. Allah ever surroundeth what they do

4:109.ar: هَٰٓأَنتُمۡ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ جَٰدَلۡتُمۡ عَنۡهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا فَمَن يُجَٰدِلُ ٱللَّهَ عَنۡهُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ أَم مَّن يَكُونُ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَكِيلࣰ ا
4:109.en: Ho! ye are they who pleaded for them in the life of the world. But who will plead with Allah for them on the Day of Resurrection, or who will then be their defender

4:110.ar: وَمَن يَعۡمَلۡ سُوٓءًا أَوۡ يَظۡلِمۡ نَفۡسَهُۥ ثُمَّ يَسۡتَغۡفِرِ ٱللَّهَ يَجِدِ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣰ ا رَّحِيمࣰ ا
4:110.en: Yet whoso doeth evil or wrongeth his own soul, then seeketh pardon of Allah, will find Allah Forgiving, Merciful

4:111.ar: وَمَن يَكۡسِبۡ إِثۡمࣰ ا فَإِنَّمَا يَكۡسِبُهُۥ عَلَىٰ نَفۡسِهِۦۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمࣰ ا
4:111.en: Whoso committeth sin committeth it only against himself. Allah is ever Knower, Wise

4:112.ar: وَمَن يَكۡسِبۡ خَطِيٓـَٔةً أَوۡ إِثۡمࣰ ا ثُمَّ يَرۡمِ بِهِۦ بَرِيٓـࣰٔ ا فَقَدِ ٱحۡتَمَلَ بُهۡتَٰنࣰ ا وَإِثۡمࣰ ا مُّبِينࣰ ا
4:112.en: And whoso committeth a delinquency or crime, then throweth (the blame) thereof upon the innocent, hath burdened himself with falsehood and a flagrant crime

4:113.ar: وَلَوۡلَا فَضۡلُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكَ وَرَحۡمَتُهُۥ لَهَمَّت طَّآئِفَةࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ أَن يُضِلُّوكَ وَمَا يُضِلُّونَ إِلَّآ أَنفُسَهُمۡۖ وَمَا يَضُرُّونَكَ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ وَأَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡكَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَعَلَّمَكَ مَا لَمۡ تَكُن تَعۡلَمُۚ وَكَانَ فَضۡلُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكَ عَظِيمࣰ ا
4:113.en: But for the grace of Allah upon thee (Muhammad), and His mercy, a party of them had resolved to mislead thee, but they will mislead only themselves and they will hurt thee not at all. Allah revealeth unto thee the Scripture and wisdom, and teacheth thee that which thou knewest not. The grace of Allah toward thee hath been infinite

11:76.ar: يَٰٓإِبۡرَٰهِيمُ أَعۡرِضۡ عَنۡ هَٰذَآۖ إِنَّهُۥ قَدۡ جَآءَ أَمۡرُ رَبِّكَۖ وَإِنَّهُمۡ ءَاتِيهِمۡ عَذَابٌ غَيۡرُ مَرۡدُودࣲ‏
11:76.en: (It was said) O Abraham! Forsake this! Lo! thy Lord's commandment hath gone forth, and lo! there cometh unto them a doom which cannot be repelled

11:37.ar: وَٱصۡنَعِ ٱلۡفُلۡكَ بِأَعۡيُنِنَا وَوَحۡيِنَا وَلَا تُخَٰطِبۡنِي فِي ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوٓاْ إِنَّهُم مُّغۡرَقُونَ

gPldp2lRWPg.title: Seerah Halaqah: The Theft of the Shield and Justice for a Jewish Neighbour (Part 2)
gPldp2lRWPg.one_line: The sons of Ubayriq steal and frame a Jewish neighbour; revelation in An-Nisa clears him, teaching that justice is owed to everyone.
gPldp2lRWPg.summary: The sheikh tells the story behind verses 105 to 113 of Surat An-Nisa. Rifa'ah, the newly Muslim uncle of Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man, had stored his winter wheat and a valuable shield, and the sons of Ubayriq broke in and stole them. Qatadah traced a trail of wheat to their house but had only suspicion. Fearing exposure, they rallied their extended family to vouch for them and planted the shield in the yard of their Jewish neighbour, Zayd ibn al-Samin. Popular opinion turned against Qatadah, and the Prophet was inclined to rule on the evidence. Then Jibril came at night with verses telling the Prophet not to plead for those who betray themselves, warning those who hide from people but not from Allah, and condemning whoever commits a sin and throws it on an innocent person. The sheikh draws two lessons. First, own your mistakes instead of blaming others; lying destroys trust and framing the innocent is among the gravest sins. Second, justice has no exceptions: the Quran cleared a non-Muslim and exposed Muslims publicly. He applies this to civil rights today, including for people whose lifestyle Muslims disagree with, and calls the community to prove the Quran's worth by living its values.

outline.heading: The Jewish neighbour and the uncle's winter supplies
outline.gist: Rifa'ah stores wheat for the winter in a shed; such stores meant survival in that season.

outline.heading: The break-in and Qatadah calms his uncle
outline.gist: The sons of Ubayriq steal the wheat and a shield; Qatadah promises his new Muslim uncle he will seek justice.

outline.heading: Following the trail: suspicion without proof
outline.gist: The trail of wheat and the smell of bread point to the thieves, but there is no hard evidence.

outline.heading: The shield and the thieves' panic
outline.gist: Seeing Qatadah investigating, they realise they are caught; the stolen shield was the most valuable item.

outline.heading: The family enlisted to lie
outline.gist: Relatives agree to vouch for them out of tribal loyalty, and Qatadah brings his case to the Prophet.

outline.heading: Framing Zayd ibn al-Samin
outline.gist: They plant the shield in the Jewish neighbour's yard and accuse him, and the shield is found there.

outline.heading: Public opinion turns; the Prophet leans toward a ruling
outline.gist: People shame Qatadah, and the Prophet, going by the evidence, is about to judge.

outline.heading: Jibril at night: judge by what Allah shows you
outline.gist: The verses tell the Prophet to judge with what Allah has shown him, not to defend traitors, and to seek forgiveness.

outline.heading: Do not plead for those who betray themselves
outline.gist: Allah does not love the treacherous; the Prophet is told not to argue on their behalf.

outline.heading: Ibrahim and Nuh also told not to argue
outline.gist: When a sin is grave, as with the people of Lut or Nuh's people, prophets are told not to plead for them.

outline.heading: Hiding from people but not from Allah
outline.gist: They plotted at night and asked their family to lie; who will defend them on the Day of Judgment?

outline.heading: Throwing your sin on an innocent person
outline.gist: Whoever commits a sin and blames someone innocent carries slander and clear sin.

outline.heading: Own your mistakes
outline.gist: Children blame siblings, but mature Muslims accept the consequences; lying is the easy way out.

outline.heading: Lying destroys trust
outline.gist: Once you lie no one can trust you; framing others is the betrayal the verses begin with.

outline.heading: Justice for a non-Muslim, announced publicly
outline.gist: Revelation came at night to clear a Jewish man and expose Muslims, even at the risk of tribal tension.

outline.heading: Civil rights for everyone, even those we disagree with
outline.gist: Muslims reject certain behaviour but never accept anyone losing their civil rights.

outline.heading: Haqq and 'adl: justice as truth in action
outline.gist: Righteousness is the highest value and justice is its practical expression.

outline.heading: Why justice deserved a public announcement
outline.gist: It was not hushed up; the verses are recited forever so we remember a non-Muslim was cleared.

outline.heading: A dynamic time of revelation
outline.gist: The end of year five and start of year six brought daily guidance on behaviour.

outline.heading: Prove the Quran by living it
outline.gist: Claiming the best book means nothing unless our society becomes loving, respectful and just.

outline.heading: Outro

48:27.ar: لَّقَدۡ صَدَقَ ٱللَّهُ رَسُولَهُ ٱلرُّءۡيَا بِٱلۡحَقِّۖ لَتَدۡخُلُنَّ ٱلۡمَسۡجِدَ ٱلۡحَرَامَ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ ءَامِنِينَ مُحَلِّقِينَ رُءُوسَكُمۡ وَمُقَصِّرِينَ لَا تَخَافُونَۖ فَعَلِمَ مَا لَمۡ تَعۡلَمُواْ فَجَعَلَ مِن دُونِ ذَٰلِكَ فَتۡحࣰ ا قَرِيبًا

bAWEYfy3rgM.title: Seerah Halaqah: Choosing Peace After the Trench (Part 3)
bAWEYfy3rgM.one_line: A preview of Hudaybiyyah: holding the initiative after the Trench, the Prophet chose peace to open Arabia to his message.
bAWEYfy3rgM.summary: In this short closing segment the sheikh previews the next class, which he calls the most important turning point in the seerah. He describes a graph of the number of Muslims: slow, steady growth until one event, after which it shoots up. After the Battle of the Trench the Confederates had fallen apart and the Prophet was now the strongest force in Arabia, able to attack Quraysh and win. Yet whenever he held the initiative and had the choice between war and peace, he chose peace. He explains why: the Arab tribes would not engage with him while Quraysh, as guardians of the Kaaba and the pilgrimage, told them to stay away. Fixing the relationship with Quraysh would let the whole peninsula listen freely, and he wanted to do this peacefully, keeping the doors of brotherhood open. A new generation of Quraysh leaders had replaced those killed or discredited; they were more reasonable in some ways but angrier and less wise. The Prophet then saw a dream of entering the Kaaba, which gave him a plan to force a peace on Quraysh, to be explained next week.

outline.heading: A turning point: the number of Muslims skyrockets
outline.gist: Growth was slow and steady until one event, after which conversions shot up.

outline.heading: Holding the initiative, he chooses peace
outline.gist: After the Trench the Prophet was the strongest force in Arabia, yet he chose peace whenever the choice was his.

outline.heading: Why peace: Quraysh's hold on the tribes
outline.gist: Tribes avoided him because Quraysh controlled the Kaaba and the pilgrimage.

outline.heading: Repair the relationship so Arabia can listen
outline.gist: He only wanted to speak freely and let people choose; peace with Quraysh would remove their fear.

outline.heading: A new generation of Quraysh leaders
outline.gist: After the old leaders fell, younger leaders were more reasonable but angrier and less wise.

outline.heading: The dream of entering the Kaaba
outline.gist: The dream gives him a plan to force peace on Quraysh, which he will explain next class.

outline.heading: Outro

FCT_5CKhA40.title: Seerah Halaqah: Events of Year Five (Part 1)
FCT_5CKhA40.one_line: Events of year five after hijrah: the Confederate alliance forms, al-Hasan is born, Zayd ibn Thabit learns Hebrew, and the Prophet marries Umm Salamah.
FCT_5CKhA40.summary: The sheikh sets the scene for the fifth year after the hijrah, which he calls the climax of the Medinan period. The Prophet's influence was growing, so Quraysh and the Jewish tribes, with Huyayy ibn Akhtab as a key organiser, united the Arabs for the first time into a force of about ten thousand. He adds that Huyayy's hostility hardened after his daughter Safiyyah dreamt of a moon falling into her lap, which was read as marriage to a prophet. He then walks through smaller events of that year. The birth of al-Hasan shows the Prophet as a joyful grandfather, and his changing Fatimah's chosen name Harb to Hasan leads into a call to be proud of strong, dignified names without arrogance. Zayd ibn Thabit, aged sixteen, learning Hebrew within days to serve as the Prophet's interpreter becomes a lesson that motivation, not talent, decides achievement, and that excuses are endless when we do not truly want something. Finally he tells Umm Salamah's story: her painful hijrah, the death of Abu Salamah, the dua for something better after a loss, and her marriage to the Prophet. He uses it to explain why the Prophet married several women, arguing the mothers of the believers received a religious and political status that elevated women in Arabia.

outline.heading: Year five: the climax of the Medinan years
outline.gist: He places the class in the fifth year after hijrah and explains how pressure had been building as the Prophet's influence spread.

outline.heading: The Arabs unite against Medina for the first time
outline.gist: Quraysh and the Jewish tribes panic and gather about ten thousand warriors from many tribes to end the Muslims.

outline.heading: Huyayy ibn Akhtab orchestrates the alliance
outline.gist: The exiled leader of Banu Nadir, who knew the Prophet was genuine but refused him out of jealousy, works with Abu Sufyan and others to build the army.

outline.heading: Safiyyah's dream of the moon
outline.gist: His daughter dreams the moon falls into her lap, is told she will marry a prophet, and his fury deepens his hostility.

outline.heading: Birth of al-Hasan: the Prophet as grandfather
outline.gist: The Prophet is overjoyed with his first grandson, a reminder of his human side after so many losses.

outline.heading: Why Fatimah chose the name Harb
outline.gist: Under constant attack, the Muslims wanted a tough generation and believed strong names produce strong people.

outline.heading: Be proud of your name
outline.gist: He urges young people not to shorten or hide unusual names, to trace their roots and carry the dignity of their names without arrogance.

outline.heading: Hasan, Husayn, Muhsin: strength without violence
outline.gist: The Prophet renames each grandson with a beautiful name meaning goodness and excellence rather than war.

outline.heading: Zayd ibn Thabit chosen as interpreter
outline.gist: After the plot of Banu Nadir, the Prophet wants someone to read and speak Hebrew and picks the gifted sixteen-year-old Zayd, later the compiler of the Quran.

outline.heading: Learning Hebrew in about sixteen days
outline.gist: Zayd returns within days able to read and write it and becomes the Prophet's personal interpreter.

outline.heading: Motivation beats talent; excuses are endless
outline.gist: Talent is wasted without motivation; people find time for what they truly want and should be honest with themselves about the rest.

outline.heading: Umm Salamah's hijrah: separated from husband and child
outline.gist: Her clan seized her son and kept her from her husband for a year until she was allowed to travel to Medina.

outline.heading: Abu Salamah's death and the dua for something better
outline.gist: The Prophet teaches the grieving widow to ask Allah to reward her in her calamity and replace it with something better.

outline.heading: Marriage to Umm Salamah
outline.gist: She could not imagine anyone better than Abu Salamah until the Prophet proposed; she became a pious and central teacher.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet married several women
outline.gist: He answers a frequent question: the Prophet was monogamous with Khadijah and his later marriages served various purposes.

outline.heading: Mothers of the believers: religious and political status
outline.gist: His wives could not be silenced or overruled because they lived with him, giving women unprecedented standing in Arabia.

outline.heading: Aishah's authority and the honour of the Prophet's wives
outline.gist: Aishah led an army and narrated over two thousand hadith; these marriages paved the way for respect of women generally.

outline.heading: Outro

33:9.en: O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see. And Allah is ever Seer of what ye do

33:10.ar: إِذۡ جَآءُوكُم مِّن فَوۡقِكُمۡ وَمِنۡ أَسۡفَلَ مِنكُمۡ وَإِذۡ زَاغَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡصَٰرُ وَبَلَغَتِ ٱلۡقُلُوبُ ٱلۡحَنَاجِرَ وَتَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلظُّنُونَا۠

98_avq4W-KM.title: Seerah Halaqah: Preparing for the Battle of the Trench (Part 2)
98_avq4W-KM.one_line: The Prophet consults the companions about the ten-thousand-strong Confederate army, adopts Salman al-Farsi's trench idea, and plans the five-kilometre trench.
98_avq4W-KM.summary: The sheikh describes the shock in Medina when news arrived that ten thousand fighters were marching on the city, while the Muslims could field about fifteen hundred. As always, the Prophet consulted his companions, and he notes that the Quran itself records their psychological state in Surat al-Ahzab. Various ideas were raised: retreating to a mountain, seeking help from northern kingdoms, or fleeing. Then Salman al-Farsi, a Persian and former slave who would never have dared speak in a traditional Arab gathering, felt respected enough to propose digging a trench. The sheikh dwells on the Prophet's open-mindedness in accepting a foreign, untested idea at an age when many people resist anything new, and insists that following the Prophet means being open to good ideas, since newness is no reason to reject something. He then explains Medina's geography with maps: lava fields to the east and west, the forts of the Jewish tribes to the south, leaving only the northern side open. He works through the trench's dimensions, the rubble piled on the Muslim side, the sixty groups of twenty-five each assigned their own stretch to dig and defend, and the ten-day deadline, which meant each man digging roughly the volume of a bedroom with simple tools.

outline.heading: News of ten thousand and the call to consult
outline.gist: The Prophet gathers the companions and asks their advice; they are stunned by the size of the army.

outline.heading: How the ten thousand were assembled
outline.gist: No tribe had such numbers; contingents from many tribes combined into one force.

outline.heading: The Quran's account of the Confederates
outline.gist: Surat al-Ahzab records the companions' fear and reactions more precisely than any retelling; he promises to explain the verses.

outline.heading: Options raised and the young sent home
outline.gist: Ideas include holding a mountain or seeking northern allies; the Prophet turns back boys too young to fight despite needing every man.

outline.heading: Every tribe sends a representative
outline.gist: Like the plot on the night of hijrah, every tribe joins so the blame is shared and no one can retaliate against all.

outline.heading: Salman al-Farsi: the man who would never have spoken
outline.gist: As a non-Arab and former slave, Salman would have been silenced in any other Arab gathering.

outline.heading: Salman feels respected enough to speak
outline.gist: He tells them that in Persia they dug a trench when attacked by a larger army.

outline.heading: The trench idea and the laughter
outline.gist: Some laugh, unsure if he is serious; the Prophet asks him to explain how it works.

outline.heading: The Prophet's open-mindedness
outline.gist: Unlike people who grow set in their ways with age, the Prophet in his late fifties welcomed a strange foreign idea.

outline.heading: Newness is no reason to reject an idea
outline.gist: Following the Prophet means listening to others' experience; being closed-minded in his name makes no sense.

outline.heading: The companions' doubts and simple tools
outline.gist: They were not builders and had only basic tools, yet the community adapted.

outline.heading: Medina's geography: the lava fields east and west
outline.gist: Deep black volcanic rock fields make the east and west impassable; he recalls dropping a stone into one in Medina.

outline.heading: The south sealed by the Jewish forts
outline.gist: With forts and huge gates in the south and a treaty with those tribes, only the north needed defending.

outline.heading: Measuring the trench: five kilometres long
outline.gist: Using maps he shows the northern gap and the length the trench needed to cover.

outline.heading: Why the width and depth mattered
outline.gist: It had to be too wide for horses to jump or planks to bridge, and deep enough that a fall was fatal.

outline.heading: Rubble piled on the Muslim side
outline.gist: The excavated earth formed a rampart for the defenders, so no real battle would happen inside the trench.

outline.heading: Sixty groups, each digging and defending its stretch
outline.gist: About sixty thousand cubic metres split among sixty groups of twenty-five, each told it would defend what it dug.

outline.heading: Leadership through knowledge of the land
outline.gist: Reviewing the map, he highlights how well the Prophet knew the geography and how carefully the plan was designed.

outline.heading: Mount Sal' and the northern line
outline.gist: He marks the mountain behind the trench that becomes central to the story.

outline.heading: Ten days: each man digs the volume of a room
outline.gist: With ten days before the army arrived, every man had to move about forty cubic metres of rocky ground by hand.

outline.heading: His own trench experiment begins
outline.gist: He starts telling how he once tried digging a similar section with ten high-school volunteers.

dTnRBFgfKUM.title: Seerah Halaqah, November 3, 2018 (Part 4): Poetry and Hunger at the Trench
dTnRBFgfKUM.one_line: Digging the trench: chanted poetry that lifted morale, the Prophet's deliberate imperfection as a leader, stones tied against hunger, and Jabir's small meal.
dTnRBFgfKUM.summary: He describes the companions digging the trench while chanting verses: a prayer asking Allah to send tranquillity and keep their feet firm against those who wanted to turn them from their faith, and the Ansar's pledge to stand by the Prophet as long as they lived. Meaningful art, he says, does exactly this: it takes people who feel beaten, few and alone and makes them believe they can do the impossible, which is why the Prophet asked for poetry while building the masjid too. When the Prophet himself recited, he broke the rhythm, and he believes this was a choice. A leader who is good at everything cannot be related to; showing people what you cannot do reminds followers that leaders are human, not gods, which keeps the relationship healthy. Very few leaders have the courage to be vulnerable this way. Yet singing could not fill empty stomachs. Working long days in the heat with almost no food, the companions tied stones against their bellies to ease the hunger, and when they showed the Prophet, he revealed two stones tied to his own. The segment ends as Jabir, seeing the Prophet's hunger, goes home to find a tiny meal of barley and meat and quietly invites him, only for the Prophet to call the whole army.

33:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَةَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ جَآءَتۡكُمۡ جُنُودࣱ فَأَرۡسَلۡنَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ رِيحࣰ ا وَجُنُودࣰ ا لَّمۡ تَرَوۡهَاۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرًا
33:9.en: O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see. And Allah is ever Seer of what ye do

33:10.ar: إِذۡ جَآءُوكُم مِّن فَوۡقِكُمۡ وَمِنۡ أَسۡفَلَ مِنكُمۡ وَإِذۡ زَاغَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡصَٰرُ وَبَلَغَتِ ٱلۡقُلُوبُ ٱلۡحَنَاجِرَ وَتَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ ٱلظُّنُونَا۠
33:10.en: When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when eyes grew wild and hearts reached to the throats, and ye were imagining vain thoughts concerning Allah

33:11.ar: هُنَالِكَ ٱبۡتُلِيَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ وَزُلۡزِلُواْ زِلۡزَالࣰ ا شَدِيدࣰ ا
33:11.en: There were the believers sorely tried, and shaken with a mighty shock

33:12.ar: وَإِذۡ يَقُولُ ٱلۡمُنَٰفِقُونَ وَٱلَّذِينَ فِي قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضࣱ مَّا وَعَدَنَا ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥٓ إِلَّا غُرُورࣰ ا
33:12.en: And when the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, were saying: Allah and His messenger promised us naught but delusion

33:13.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَت طَّآئِفَةࣱ مِّنۡهُمۡ يَٰٓأَهۡلَ يَثۡرِبَ لَا مُقَامَ لَكُمۡ فَٱرۡجِعُواْۚ وَيَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُ فَرِيقࣱ مِّنۡهُمُ ٱلنَّبِيَّ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّ بُيُوتَنَا عَوۡرَةࣱ وَمَا هِيَ بِعَوۡرَةٍۖ إِن يُرِيدُونَ إِلَّا فِرَارࣰ ا
33:13.en: And when a party of them said: O folk of Yathrib! There is no stand (possible) for you, therefor turn back. And certain of them (even) sought permission of the Prophet, saying: Our homes lie open (to the enemy). And they lay not open. They but wished to flee

33:14.ar: وَلَوۡ دُخِلَتۡ عَلَيۡهِم مِّنۡ أَقۡطَارِهَا ثُمَّ سُئِلُواْ ٱلۡفِتۡنَةَ لَأٓتَوۡهَا وَمَا تَلَبَّثُواْ بِهَآ إِلَّا يَسِيرࣰ ا
33:14.en: If the enemy had entered from all sides and they had been exhorted to treachery, they would have committed it, and would have hesitated thereupon but little

33:15.ar: وَلَقَدۡ كَانُواْ عَٰهَدُواْ ٱللَّهَ مِن قَبۡلُ لَا يُوَلُّونَ ٱلۡأَدۡبَٰرَۚ وَكَانَ عَهۡدُ ٱللَّهِ مَسۡـُٔولࣰ ا
33:15.en: And verily they had already sworn unto Allah that they would not turn their backs (to the foe). An oath to Allah must be answered for

33:16.ar: قُل لَّن يَنفَعَكُمُ ٱلۡفِرَارُ إِن فَرَرۡتُم مِّنَ ٱلۡمَوۡتِ أَوِ ٱلۡقَتۡلِ وَإِذࣰ ا لَّا تُمَتَّعُونَ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ ا
33:16.en: Say: Flight will not avail you if ye flee from death or killing, and then ye dwell in comfort but a little while

33:17.ar: قُلۡ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يَعۡصِمُكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ إِنۡ أَرَادَ بِكُمۡ سُوٓءًا أَوۡ أَرَادَ بِكُمۡ رَحۡمَةࣰۚ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ لَهُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَلِيࣰّ ا وَلَا نَصِيرࣰ ا
33:17.en: Say: Who is he who can preserve you from Allah if He intendeth harm for you, or intendeth mercy for you. They will not find that they have any friend or helper other than Allah

33:18.ar: ۞قَدۡ يَعۡلَمُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنكُمۡ وَٱلۡقَآئِلِينَ لِإِخۡوَٰنِهِمۡ هَلُمَّ إِلَيۡنَاۖ وَلَا يَأۡتُونَ ٱلۡبَأۡسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
33:18.en: Allah already knoweth those of you who hinder, and those who say unto their brethren: "Come ye hither unto us!" and they come not to the stress of battle save a little

JbMl_jaeJac.title: Seerah Halaqah, October 20, 2018 (Part 3): Caring for the Overlooked and the Gathering of the Confederates
JbMl_jaeJac.one_line: The Prophet's care for Jabir and the forgotten, then how Huyayy ibn Akhtab united Arabia's tribes into a 10,000-strong army against Medina.
JbMl_jaeJac.summary: He finishes the return from Dhat al-Riqa'. The Prophet asked Jabir about his marriage and learned he had married an experienced woman to help raise his nine sisters; he held the army outside Medina for a night so families would not be caught unprepared; and he paid Jabir for his camel and then gave it back. All of this shows a leader who cared about the small details of people's lives, and especially about those others overlooked. Societies fail, he argues, when the fortunate forget the weak, so he sets an exercise: at school or work, find someone isolated and make them feel valued. He then opens the Battle of the Trench. Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who had chosen lifelong enmity after meeting the Prophet, went from tribe to tribe building an alliance, even telling Quraysh their idol worship was better than Islam. He stresses that the Prophet never punished anyone for words alone, only for violence. Tribes that had feuded for centuries united, gathering around ten thousand against perhaps 1,500 fighters in Medina. Enemies will always act like enemies, he says; the failure is ours if we are not prepared, practically and intellectually, to defend our faith. He asks the audience to read the opening pages of Surat al-Ahzab.

outline.heading: Jabir's marriage and his nine sisters
outline.gist: Asked about his marriage, Jabir explained he chose an older wife who could help raise his sisters.

outline.heading: Halting outside Medina so families could prepare
outline.gist: The Prophet sent word ahead and camped a night so wives were not caught off guard by husbands returning after weeks away.

outline.heading: Jabir remembers that moment
outline.gist: Years later, wealthy, Jabir said he would give everything to return to that day with the Prophet.

outline.heading: Women on the expeditions
outline.gist: Women took part in campaigns, handling medical care, food and clothing, and the army waited a day before entering.

outline.heading: He cared about the small details
outline.gist: The Prophet asked about people's marriages and homes because he wanted them to make choices that would make them happy and functional.

outline.heading: Paying for the camel and giving it back
outline.gist: At home the Prophet sent Jabir the price and returned the camel too; he never wanted it, only to help.

outline.heading: Societies fail when the weak are forgotten
outline.gist: When the fortunate forget the less fortunate, communities fall; the Prophet went looking for such people and pulled them into conversation.

outline.heading: An exercise: find the isolated person
outline.gist: At school or work, look for someone without friends or social ease and do something to lift them.

outline.heading: The enemies realise they must unite
outline.gist: Quraysh and the exiled tribes understood none could defeat the Muslims alone.

outline.heading: Huyayy ibn Akhtab chooses enmity
outline.gist: He and his brother studied the Prophet against their scriptures' description and walked out resolved to be his enemy for life.

outline.heading: Building the alliance and the oath at the Kaaba
outline.gist: Huyayy went from tribe to tribe recruiting, and the leaders pressed themselves to the Kaaba swearing to stand together until Islam was destroyed.

outline.heading: No one punished for words
outline.gist: When companions asked about harsh critics, the Prophet answered speech with speech; no one was executed for what they said alone.

outline.heading: Idol worship better than Islam?
outline.gist: To win Quraysh, Huyayy told them their religion was better than Muhammad's, though he knew both revelations shared an origin.

outline.heading: Assembling the Confederates
outline.gist: Quraysh brought 4,000 with horses and camels, Ghatafan thousands more, and every tribe sent some fighters, for around 10,000 in all.

outline.heading: Rivals unite; Muslims lack the will
outline.gist: Tribes that had feuded for centuries united to fight, while Muslims today lack that willingness to work together.

outline.heading: Enemies will be enemies; prepare yourself
outline.gist: There is no point resenting enemies; if they harm you because you never built your narrative or defence of the deen, that is your fault.

outline.heading: Medina's real strength
outline.gist: Of the city's population only about 1,500 could fight, facing 10,000.

outline.heading: The name al-Ahzab
outline.gist: His intelligence warned him early; the battle is called the Trench or the Confederates, and he asks them to read the opening pages of the surah.
